extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literary criticism; critics and writers evaluating allegory, poetry, and Restoration drama
extracted.subtask_description: Critical guidance for evaluating allegorical narrative, poetic imagination, and Restoration drama—what makes an allegory or dramatic work effective, morally defensible, and stylistically valuable. Emphasises imagination, personification, language register, historical reference, and moral consequences of representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegorical consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the correspondence between outward sign and thing signified is preserved consistently across a long allegory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay notes that 'no human ingenuity could produce such a centipede as a long allegory in which the correspondence... should be exactly preserved.' Minute scrutiny will detect inconsistencies, and such inconsistencies are largely unavoidable. The best practice is to present a succession of analogies, each separately striking and happy, rather than to force exact harmony throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification made human
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which abstractions and qualities are rendered as vivid, individualized characters rather than mere abstract labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praised in Bunyan: 'Bunyan is almost the only writer who ever gave to the abstract the interest of the concrete.' A dialogue between two qualities in his work 'has more dramatic effect than a dialogue between two human beings in most plays.' Effective personification makes generalities feel like real people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative transformation of abstractions
rubrics_metrics.description: The poetical faculty that reverses the abstracting process—turning metaphysical principles into sensuous, life-like forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Shelley: 'The Spirit of Beauty, the Principle of Good, the Principle of Evil... ceased to be abstractions. They took shape and colour.' This reversal (making individuals out of generalities) is presented as a strong sign of true poetical power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of simple, homely vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the language and vocabulary of common people—short words and plain dialect to convey meaning precisely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bunyan's 'vocabulary is the vocabulary of the common people' and 'several pages which do not contain a single word of more than two syllables.' The essay argues this homely dialect is perfectly sufficient for 'magnificence, for pathos, for vehement exhortation, for subtle disquisition' and shows the richness of English without needing learned diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occasional doctrinal or pulpit-like digressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages where the allegory is dropped in favour of direct religious ejaculations, sermons, or disquisitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These moments — 'he altogether drops the allegory, and puts into the mouth of his pilgrims religious ejaculations and disquisitions' — are acknowledged as inconsistent with strict allegory and objectionable to some critics, yet the reviewer argues they 'add... much of its charm' and are hard to spare because they bring solemn and affecting subjects through the veil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/contextual dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which characters, scenes, or references require contemporary or historical knowledge for full comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some parts (e.g., Mr. Greatheart) are 'fully comprehended and enjoyed only by persons familiar with the history of the times.' Reliance on such knowledge may limit accessibility, though it can enrich meaning for informed readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical allegory as political critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Effectiveness of allegory in satirising political or legal practices by drawing parallels between fictional proceedings and real historical events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The trial of Faithful is read as satire of state trials under Charles II: the licence of witnesses, shameless partiality of the judge, and prejudiced jury echo real abuses. Allegorical trials are effective when parallels to real cases are clear and pointed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral association and representational responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether immoral behaviour is presented in constant connection with what is attractive, thereby making vice seem desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer warns: 'morality is deeply interested in this, that what is immoral shall not be presented to the imagination of the young and susceptible in constant connection with what is attractive.' Works that systematically associate vice with attractiveness risk promoting immorality and deserve moral scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of a conventional or fictional world
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the fictional world is clearly conventional (distinct from real life) or closely mirrors reality, affecting the moral impact of its representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conventional worlds (Fenelon, Southey) are unobjectionable because so unlike reality that imitation is unlikely. But when a work creates a conventional world closely resembling the actual world (as in Wycherley/Congreve), representing vice as laudable becomes dangerous because real readers may emulate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire of social types and character-naming
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of allegorical character-types (By-ends, Mr. Two-tongues, etc.) to satirise particular social behaviors and public figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegorical names and caricatures often mirror real social and political types; they serve to expose hypocrisy, opportunism, or corruption and can increase the narrative's relevance and bite, especially when readers can recognise the targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial sympathy and tonal compassion
rubrics_metrics.description: Predominant tone of tenderness or compassion toward afflicted, timid, or harassed minds within religious or moral narratives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bunyan's work is described as having 'a feeling of tenderness for weak, timid, and harassed minds,' which gives the allegory a calm and soothing religious form and makes it particularly consoling to readers in distress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value as a vehicle for language instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Usefulness of a text as a study object for mastering the English language and expressive clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay asserts Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress is 'invaluable as a study to every person who wishes to obtain a wide command over the English language,' showing how plain diction can express exact meaning and that English has abundant native resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of conjugal fidelity and social norms
rubrics_metrics.description: How a drama treats important social virtues (e.g., conjugal fidelity): whether as a serious crime when breached or as a fashionable grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts Elizabethan dramatists (who punish or ridicule seducers) with Restoration dramatists (who often render adultery a mark of breeding). The critic treats the Restoration tendency — making adultery an aspect of gentlemanly grace — as morally corrosive and artistically culpable when it systematically glamorises vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing poetic genius against doctrinal or ethical error
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether extraordinary imaginative or poetic power can redeem metaphysical, ethical, or doctrinal absurdities in a writer's work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges that some of Shelley's theories were 'absurd and pernicious' yet argues that his imaginative power justifies applying terms like 'bard' and 'inspiration' to him; thus critical judgment may weigh imaginative merits against theoretical flaws.
